audit_notes: Parameters are physically plausible. Checks: (1) slip length of a post-type shear-free surface b = L*(0.325/sqrt(phi_s) - 0.44) = 3e-4*0.588 = 1.76e-4 m, i.e. b+ = 46 in viscous units; this ideal value is not reachable in seawater because surfactants immobilise the interface, so the formulator's interface_mobility_factor 0.075 (effective slip 1.3e-5 m, b+ about 3.5) is kept as a conservative, literature-informed correction. (2) The gas layer itself: the air-layer shear resistance (b limited to h_a*mu_w/mu_a = 5e-4*67 = 3.3e-2 m) is not limiting. (3) Stability: Laplace pressure 2*0.072/3e-4 = 480 Pa exceeds rms wall-pressure fluctuations (about 2.5*tau_w = 250 Pa) but not peak fluctuations in waves or slamming; hydrostatic compression at 10 m draft (100 kPa) is only survivable with the air feed. Gas demand of 1e-6 m3/(m2 s) is 10 L/s for 1e4 m2 at 2 bar, a compressor of a few kW, small compared with a 10 MW propulsion plant. (4) Structural: silicone hairs of 0.5 mm height and about 50 um diameter under 100 Pa shear deflect negligibly (tip deflection << 1 um); cleaning brushes would destroy them. (5) Model: the turbulent boundary layer is represented by an equivalent laminar Couette gap H = nu*U/u_tau^2 = 1.2e-4 m that reproduces the smooth-wall shear mu*U/H = 100 Pa; with a Navier slip condition tau/tau0 = 1/(1 + b_eff/H). This first-order model gives about 10 %; a log-law shift argument gives about 19 %, so the simulated value is conservative. Not captured: fouling of the hairs and the air-water interface, which is the dominant long-term risk; air loss in waves; the air-feed energy. Baseline: the same wall without a gas layer (interface_mobility_factor = 0, no slip), i.e. a clean smooth hull.
